issues.subcategory: retrospective design mislabeled as prospective/real-time prediction
issues.description: The study reconstructs past episodes and then analyzes archived SMS data, but the manuscript repeatedly frames this as prospective, predictive, and real-time risk identification. Timestamped messages preceding a retrospectively identified event do not make the design prospective, and no prospective prediction or real-time validation was conducted. This matters because performance in retrospective case-crossover analyses can substantially overestimate usefulness for real-time clinical prediction.
issues.quote: By reconstructing the timeline of recent suicidal behaviors through a retrospective clinical interview, we utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt

issues.subcategory: inconsistent suicide-attempt episode window
issues.description: The manuscript inconsistently defines the suicide-attempt episode as one week versus two weeks. The abstract, overview, analysis plan, and conclusions refer to two weeks before an attempt, but the interview procedure says the attempt episode used the one-week period prior to the attempt. This ambiguity directly affects which SMS messages were analyzed and undermines reproducibility and interpretation of temporal slopes.
issues.quote: Episodes included: 1) past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the one-week period prior to the attempt as a “suicide attempt episode”; 2) two-week episodes of suicide ideation

issues.subcategory: two-week window coded as -14 to 0
issues.description: The time variable is described as ranging from -14 to 0, which includes 15 calendar values if both endpoints are included. This conflicts with the repeated description of a two-week or 14-day period and is especially consequential because the key findings are episode-type-by-day interactions.
issues.quote: day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0)

issues.subcategory: data-driven temporal window selection
issues.description: The manuscript states that the episode length was chosen conservatively but also says the optimal time window was assessed empirically using visual inspection of the same data. Choosing or justifying the analysis window after inspecting temporal patterns creates circularity and inflates the chance of detecting apparent slope effects, especially in a small exploratory study with many outcomes.
issues.quote: The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures to identify when the rate of change appeared to be most pronounced.

issues.subcategory: broad and subjective definition of suicide attempt
issues.description: The main outcome labeled as a suicide attempt includes actual, interrupted, aborted, and even self-endorsed events with no enacted physical attempt. This conflates suicide attempts with high-intent ideation/planning and aborted behavior. Because the stated goal is identifying markers preceding suicide attempts, including non-attempt events threatens construct validity and may change the observed language patterns.
issues.quote: Note that reported ‘suicide attempts’ also included incidents in which no physical attempt was enacted but in which participants considered their planning or actions to constitute a higher level of suicidal intent than ‘suicide ideation’ so they subjectively endorsed making an attempt on the screener questions.

issues.subcategory: low objective lethality/physical harm in attempt episodes
issues.description: Most events classified as attempt episodes did not involve physical harm, and only a minority involved any action causing harm. This further indicates that the primary 'high-risk' condition may not represent enacted suicide attempts, limiting conclusions about detecting imminent risk of actual suicidal behavior.
issues.quote: Based on participants’ description of the objective lethality of the attempt, 29% of incidents involved some action being taken in which some physical harm was caused ... while 71% of incidents did not result in any physical harm

issues.subcategory: impossible/inconsistent number of attempts with SMS data
issues.description: The manuscript says 27 participants had SMS data and all had data from at least one reported suicide attempt, which implies at least 27 attempt episodes with SMS data. It then states that there were only 21 attempts with corresponding SMS data. These numbers cannot both be true unless different definitions are being used, but no explanation is provided.
issues.quote: Among these 27 participants, all had data from at least one reported suicide attempt. ... Among the 21 attempts with corresponding SMS data

issues.subcategory: inconsistent usable-SMS sample size across sections
issues.description: The power section refers to only 20 participants/attempts with collected usable SMS data, whereas the results state SMS data came from 27 participants. This inconsistency affects the apparent analytic sample size and power.
issues.quote: 30 suicide attempters (representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect)

issues.subcategory: large unaddressed episode-level missingness
issues.description: Less than half of identified episodes contained SMS data. The manuscript does not provide episode-type-specific missingness, reasons for missingness by condition, or sensitivity analyses showing that episodes with SMS were comparable to those without. Because missingness likely depends on recency, phone ownership, platform use, and episode type, mixed models do not solve the problem unless missingness assumptions are justified.
issues.quote: Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants.

issues.subcategory: participant-level exclusion from SMS analyses not characterized
issues.description: Thirty-three participants were enrolled, but only 27 contributed SMS data. The manuscript does not compare participants with versus without usable SMS data or explain how excluding six participants may bias estimates. Attrition is particularly important here because access to historical text data is linked to device type, recency, socioeconomic factors, and potentially clinical history.
issues.quote: A sample of 33 participants with at least one reported past suicide attempt were recruited ... Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants.

issues.subcategory: nonrandom missingness from device encryption and backups
issues.description: The manuscript documents technical barriers that prevented SMS extraction, especially among iPhone users and participants without old phones or backup passwords. These are not random missing data mechanisms, yet the analysis plan implies mixed-effects models adequately handle missingness. Nonrandom availability of messages can bias episode comparisons.
issues.quote: a number of iPhone users had encryption settings on their phones that prevented third-party iPhone software from accessing text data

issues.subcategory: selection bias from requiring historical digital-data access
issues.description: Eligibility required access to personal messaging data dating back before suicidal events. This excludes people without consistent phone ownership, people who deleted messages, those using unsupported platforms, and those with older attempts. The resulting sample may be systematically different from the population of suicide attempters.
issues.quote: Inclusion criteria included: ... availability of and access to personal messaging data dating back prior to significant life events (e.g., suicide attempt)

issues.subcategory: restricted young mostly female college sample
issues.description: The sample was predominantly female, White, and college-aged, recruited from one community/participant pool. Findings from this group should not be generalized to older adults, males, non-college populations, clinical inpatients, veterans, or people who die by suicide. The manuscript acknowledges some limitations but still makes broad claims about suicide risk and monitoring tools.
issues.quote: Most of the participants were female, White, and college-aged.

issues.subcategory: exclusion of currently high-risk individuals
issues.description: Participants with high or imminent current suicide risk were excluded. This limits generalizability to precisely the population for whom real-time suicide-risk detection would be most clinically relevant.
issues.quote: Any participants with intense thoughts of suicide who were determined to be at “high risk” or “imminent risk” for suicidal behavior ... were excluded from study participation and referred for clinical care.

issues.subcategory: incoming messages may contaminate participant-language measures
issues.description: The manuscript does not clearly state whether LIWC sentiment/self-focus analyses were restricted to outgoing messages authored by participants. Because all SMS data were downloaded and analyzed, incoming messages from other people may have contributed to psychological-language scores. If so, the measures partly reflect correspondents’ language rather than the participant’s state; if not, the restriction is not reported clearly enough for replication.
issues.quote: all available SMS data from each device were downloaded ... Across all episodes, 189,478 text messages were collected and analyzed

issues.subcategory: first-person pronouns used as rumination/self-focus proxy
issues.description: The study treats singular first-person pronoun use as an indicator of rumination/self-focus. Pronoun frequency is an indirect and context-sensitive linguistic feature, especially in brief SMS exchanges, and may reflect conversational topic, recipient, or grammar rather than maladaptive self-focus or rumination.
issues.quote: we tested whether use of first-person pronouns (as an indicator of rumination) was greater prior to suicide attempts

issues.subcategory: social engagement operationalized as sent/received ratio
issues.description: The interpersonal theory constructs of thwarted belongingness and perceived burdensomeness are operationalized using counts and ratios of sent versus received messages. This is a weak proxy: high or low outgoing/incoming ratios can reflect availability, phone habits, relationship conflict, group texts, or platform switching rather than belongingness, burdensomeness, or disengagement.
issues.quote: decreased social engagement (i.e., lower ratio of sent vs. received text messages)

issues.subcategory: positive versus typical mood inconsistency
issues.description: The comparator episode is described elsewhere as positive mood, but the interview procedure defines it as typical mood, neither positive nor negative. These are different constructs and may have different language profiles. This inconsistency undermines the interpretation of the 'positive' comparison condition in the tables and figures.
issues.quote: two-week episode of typical mood (i.e., neither particularly positive nor negative mood and no ideation or attempt)

issues.subcategory: depressed mood conflated with high stress
issues.description: The depressed comparison condition includes either depressed mood or high stress. Depression and stress are distinct constructs with potentially different language, social behavior, and suicide-risk implications. Combining them may obscure or create differences relative to attempt episodes.
issues.quote: two-week episodes of depressed mood or high stress (not resulting in suicide ideation or attempt)

issues.subcategory: risk hierarchy assumed rather than validated
issues.description: The manuscript treats attempt, ideation, depressed, and positive/typical episodes as ordered risk states. However, depressed/high-stress episodes can involve elevated suicide risk even without reported ideation, and aborted/interrupted 'attempt' episodes may overlap conceptually with ideation. The assumed ordinal risk classification is central to interpretation but not independently validated.
issues.quote: attempt episodes were considered “high risk,” ideation episodes were considered “moderate risk,” and depressed and positive episodes were considered “minimal/no risk.”

issues.subcategory: retrospective recall of episode dates and states
issues.description: Episode classification and day-level timing depend on participants retrospectively recalling dates and psychological states. Even a few days of error is consequential when the main analysis estimates daily temporal slopes immediately preceding attempts.
issues.quote: participants were asked to identify a number of specific events or episodes in the past and the calendar dates during which the episodes took place

issues.subcategory: date uncertainty problematic for temporal slope analyses
issues.description: The manuscript reports that some episode dates may be off by a few days, yet the key findings depend on detecting changes over days. No sensitivity analyses are reported to assess whether slope findings are robust to plausible date misclassification.
issues.quote: rating 90.3% of episodes as ‘very certain’ (i.e., exact days) or ‘somewhat certain’ (i.e., may be off by a few days)

issues.subcategory: unclear selection of episodes when more than three existed
issues.description: Participants could report up to three episodes per type, but no rule is given for which episodes were selected when more than three existed. This creates potential selection bias and researcher/participant degrees of freedom, especially if more memorable, recent, or severe episodes were preferentially chosen.
issues.quote: For each episode type, we asked about a maximum of three episodes (e.g., three suicide attempts if participant has three or more lifetime attempts).

issues.subcategory: lack of independent verification of suicide events
issues.description: Suicide attempts and episode categories were based on participant report and subjective interpretation, without corroboration from medical records, collateral informants, or blinded clinical adjudication. Misclassification of the outcome and comparison periods can bias within-person contrasts.
issues.quote: classification of episode type depended on participants’ interpretations of whether their behaviors qualified as a specific type of event

issues.subcategory: interviewer not described as blinded and may influence episode classification
issues.description: The experimenter assisted with data collection and interviewed participants about episodes. The manuscript does not describe interviewer blinding, standardized adjudication, or reliability checks. Knowledge of study aims could influence probing, classification, or selection of episodes.
issues.quote: participants were interviewed by the experimenter and asked to identify a number of episodes

issues.subcategory: uncontrolled time-varying confounding
issues.description: Within-subject comparisons reduce stable between-person confounding but do not address time-varying confounds such as relationship crises, substance use, medication changes, treatment, academic stress, seasonality, age, platform changes, or recipient changes. These factors could drive both language changes and suicide-risk episodes, limiting causal or mechanistic interpretations.
issues.quote: episode type serving as our main predictor variable and language characteristics of text messages during the episodes as the outcome variables

issues.subcategory: associational findings overinterpreted as biomarkers/predictors
issues.description: The study identifies retrospective associations between language features and episode labels, but repeatedly describes them as biomarkers or predictors of risk. Biomarker and prediction claims require prospective validation, out-of-sample performance, calibration, and clinically meaningful decision thresholds, none of which are provided.
issues.quote: Results suggest private electronic communication has the potential to provide real-time digital markers of suicide risk.

issues.subcategory: likelihood-ratio versus Wald chi-square confusion
issues.description: The analysis plan conflates likelihood-ratio tests and Wald chi-square tests. These are different inferential procedures with different assumptions and test statistics. Ambiguity about which was used impairs reproducibility and interpretation of p-values.
issues.quote: Likelihood-ratio (Wald chi-square) tests were performed to compare goodness of fit for models including and excluding the fixed effect of episode type.

issues.subcategory: incorrect p-value for sadness omnibus test
issues.description: The text reports 2(3)=8.74, p=.003, but the table reports p=.033, and chi-square with 3 degrees of freedom and statistic 8.74 corresponds to approximately p=.033, not .003. This is a direct statistical reporting error affecting whether the result appears stronger than it is.
issues.quote: there was a significant effect of episode type on use of sad words, 2(3)=8.74, p=.003

issues.subcategory: iatrogenic-effect direction reversed
issues.description: The reported means show desire to die increased from pre to post, and Table 1 reports a positive change, yet the text says it significantly decreased. This is an internal contradiction and potentially important because the study involves suicide-risk assessment procedures.
issues.quote: desire to die from pre (M=0.82, SD=1.10) to post (M=1.03, SD=0.90) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033

issues.subcategory: discussion claims anxiety difference not supported by results
issues.description: The discussion states that high-risk periods were associated with greater anxiety and sadness, but the results section says anxiety did not significantly differ by episode type. This overstates the mean-difference findings.
issues.quote: results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness

issues.subcategory: message-level pseudoreplication/effective sample size inflation
issues.description: The analyses use individual SMS messages as observations to maximize variance, but the inferential target is episode type within participants. With 189,478 messages but only 27 participants with SMS data and a limited number of episodes, message-level modeling risks inflated precision if within-day, within-conversation, within-recipient, and within-episode dependence is not fully modeled.
issues.quote: This approach also allowed us to maximize sources of variance by analyzing on the message level rather than only mean values by episode

issues.subcategory: random slopes omitted in key interaction models
issues.description: The primary temporal models test within-subject episode-type-by-time interactions, but the final models omitted all random slopes due to nonconvergence. Omitting random slopes for within-subject predictors can produce anti-conservative tests and inflated Type I error, especially for interaction effects that are the central findings.
issues.quote: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, no random slopes were included in the final model.

issues.subcategory: inappropriate LMM for count outcomes
issues.description: Counts of outgoing and incoming messages are nonnegative integer count outcomes, likely skewed and overdispersed. The manuscript states these were modeled as raw continuous variables in linear mixed-effects models, without reporting diagnostics or considering Poisson/negative-binomial alternatives.
issues.quote: For outcome variables that were not proportion scores (e.g., number of messages sent per day), the raw continuous variable was used in a linear mixed-effects model (LMM), using the “lmer” function.

issues.subcategory: binomial word-count model assumptions not addressed
issues.description: LIWC category counts are modeled as binomial successes/failures within messages. This assumes a well-defined denominator and independent Bernoulli trials for words, but words within a message are linguistically dependent and rare categories may be zero-inflated/overdispersed. The manuscript does not report overdispersion checks, zero-inflation handling, or sensitivity analyses.
issues.quote: These LIWC percentage scores were converted into counts and then entered as proportions in our models (i.e., number of words in a given text message belonging to versus not belonging to the LIWC category)

issues.subcategory: raw ratios may be undefined or highly skewed
issues.description: The social-engagement outcomes include ratios of sent versus received words/messages. The manuscript does not explain how days or episodes with zero incoming or zero outgoing messages were handled, whether ratios were transformed, or whether extreme ratios influenced results.
issues.quote: Ratio sent vs. received words ... Ratio sent vs. received messages

issues.subcategory: insufficient mixed-model specification
issues.description: The manuscript does not provide full model formulas, contrast coding for episode type, centering/scaling of day, optimizer settings, convergence/singularity diagnostics, treatment of nesting/crossing, or denominator degrees-of-freedom method for LMM tests. These details are necessary to reproduce the analyses and evaluate the validity of the reported p-values.
issues.quote: A series of mixed-effects models were performed with episode type as a within-subject fixed effect (4 levels: attempt, ideation, depressed, positive) and the language feature of interest as the outcome variable.

issues.subcategory: unclear p-value method for lmer t-tests
issues.description: The manuscript reports t statistics and p-values for LMM pairwise comparisons but does not specify how degrees of freedom or p-values were obtained. The lme4 lmer function does not provide default p-values for fixed effects, so the inferential method must be reported.
issues.quote: pairwise comparisons between each of the episode types (using z and t statistics for binary/proportion and continuous outcome variables, respectively)

issues.subcategory: effect-size reporting unclear and incomplete
issues.description: The manuscript treats beta coefficients as effect sizes and describes them as standardized values in log-odds units, but it is unclear how standardization was performed. Odds ratios, confidence intervals, predicted probabilities, or marginal effects would be more interpretable, especially for rare LIWC categories and interactions.
issues.quote: Here, β (standardized values of the model parameter estimates in log odds units) are reported and serve as effect sizes.

issues.subcategory: many tests without multiplicity control
issues.description: The study tests many LIWC and social-engagement outcomes, mean and slope models, and multiple pairwise contrasts. Several key findings have p-values near .05. The authors explicitly chose not to correct for multiple comparisons, increasing the probability that reported significant effects are false positives.
issues.quote: our analyses involved running a fairly large number of tests, which potentially increases the chances of rejecting the null hypothesis due to the sheer number of tests ... we decided not to artificially suppress Type I error (i.e., using a multiple comparisons correction)

issues.subcategory: exploratory analyses presented alongside a priori language
issues.description: The manuscript says predictors were selected a priori, but also notes that numerous aspects were exploratory and that alternate data-subset analyses were performed in supplements. Without preregistration or a clearly fixed analysis plan, there are substantial researcher degrees of freedom in variable selection, time-window definition, inclusion criteria, and model specification.
issues.quote: Numerous aspects of this research were exploratory by nature.

issues.subcategory: no preregistration information
issues.description: The authors provide OSF materials but do not report a preregistered protocol or analysis plan. Given the exploratory nature, many outcomes, flexible time windows, model convergence changes, and supplemental alternate analyses, absence of preregistration limits confidence that reported analyses were not selected after seeing the data.
issues.quote: full screening surveys and other study materials are available on OSF at https://osf.io/9f3v2/

issues.subcategory: underpowered and unstable subgroup/episode estimates
issues.description: The study is explicitly powered only for large effects, with very few participants and attempt episodes. The significant findings, especially interaction and pairwise effects, are therefore likely unstable and vulnerable to both Type I and Type II errors. The power analysis is also not well aligned with the multilevel longitudinal GLMMs actually used.
issues.quote: Therefore, it should be noted that the study was underpowered to detect small- or medium-sized effects and therefore prone to Type II error.

issues.subcategory: power analysis based on mismatched prior designs and tests
issues.description: The power analysis relies on large between-subject effect sizes from prior LIWC or social-support studies and on chi-square/Cramer's V assumptions, despite this study using within-subject mixed models and temporal interactions. This makes the stated power justification weak and potentially misleading.
issues.quote: we conducted a power analysis based on the assumption of large effect sizes (though no prior studies have examined within-subjects differences, which may or may not vary substantially from between-subjects comparisons)

issues.subcategory: LIWC single-word sentiment limitations in SMS
issues.description: LIWC dictionary counts may not validly capture sentiment in short, informal SMS messages containing slang, sarcasm, abbreviations, emojis, negation, and context-dependent meanings. The authors acknowledge this limitation, but it directly affects the validity of the main constructs and conclusions.
issues.quote: examining single words in isolation can fail to capture the semantic context of the word (e.g., “not happy” would count as “positive emotion” because negation is not accounted for)

issues.subcategory: insufficient reporting of episode counts by type
issues.description: The manuscript reports total episodes and average episodes per type but does not provide clear counts of usable SMS episodes by episode type, participant contribution by condition, or whether all participants contributed all conditions. This is necessary to evaluate imbalance, estimability of within-person contrasts, and whether results are driven by a small subset.
issues.quote: Participants reported and had SMS data for on average approximately 1.5 episodes for each episode type.

issues.subcategory: unclear handling of overlapping or adjacent episodes
issues.description: The manuscript does not state whether episode windows could overlap, how overlapping SMS messages were assigned, or whether ideation/depressed/positive periods were temporally separated from attempts. Overlap would violate condition independence and contaminate comparisons.
issues.quote: A total of 3 to 12 episodes were collected for each participant depending on the presence and number of reported events.

issues.subcategory: chronological/platform confounding across historical episodes
issues.description: Episodes may have occurred at different ages and calendar periods, while texting habits, devices, relationships, and platforms changed over time. The design does not appear to match comparison episodes to attempt episodes by calendar time or phone/platform context, so temporal or technological changes could masquerade as risk-related language differences.
issues.quote: Participants were asked to bring into the lab as many other devices as they thought might contain digital data (e.g., laptop with iTunes backup, older phone)

issues.subcategory: SMS may be incomplete due to platform substitution
issues.description: The study analyzes SMS only, while participants may use Facebook, Gmail, Hangouts, Twitter, Snapchat, iMessage-specific features, or other platforms differentially over time and by social context. The manuscript does not quantify what proportion of participants' communication SMS represented during each episode.
issues.quote: Additional forms of personal digital data, including phone call history, Google data (Gmail, Hangouts, and Chrome browser history), Facebook messages, and Twitter messages, were collected for the purposes of future analyses but are not part of the current study.

issues.subcategory: no non-attempter or clinical control group
issues.description: The within-subject design is useful for comparing episodes among attempters, but it cannot determine whether identified language patterns are specific to suicide attempters versus general distress, crises, or young adult communication patterns. This limits claims that the markers identify suicide risk rather than within-person emotional fluctuation.
issues.quote: By comparing multiple periods of high vs. low suicide risk, all within a sample of suicide attempters

issues.subcategory: nonfatal attempters extrapolated toward suicide prevention broadly
issues.description: The sample necessarily excludes people who died by suicide and mostly includes nonlethal or aborted/interrupted events. Although acknowledged, the manuscript still frames implications for preventing suicide broadly. Markers of nonfatal/self-reported attempt episodes may not generalize to suicide deaths.
issues.quote: logistics of accessing and downloading communication data necessitated enrolling participants with non-lethal attempts

issues.subcategory: digital biomarker terminology premature
issues.description: The manuscript uses the language of digital biomarkers/phenotyping, but the measures are retrospective, unvalidated proxies with no demonstrated diagnostic accuracy, reliability, specificity, or prospective clinical utility. The term 'biomarker' may overstate the evidentiary status of the findings.
issues.quote: identify and better understand real-time patterns in communication unique to periods preceding suicide attempts

issues.subcategory: privacy/third-party consent not sufficiently detailed
issues.description: The study downloads private SMS conversations, which include messages from nonparticipant correspondents. The manuscript notes IRB approval and secure storage but does not explain whether or how privacy interests of third parties were addressed, which is important for replication and ethical evaluation of the method.
issues.quote: Following the lab session, the raw downloaded text data were transferred to and stored on a secure server intended for the storage of sensitive information. This data storage plan was reviewed and approved by the IRB.

issues.subcategory: risk-assessment item wording and thresholds inconsistent
issues.description: The risk protocol alternates between 'desire to die' and 'desire to hurt self' and uses different thresholds at screening and lab assessment. This creates ambiguity about how current risk was measured and managed.
issues.quote: minimal or no current desire to die (i.e., less than or equal to 5 on a 0-10 Likert scale and no current suicide plan/intent) ... score greater than 3 on desire to hurt self question

issues.subcategory: omnibus significant death interaction followed by no significant attempt contrasts
issues.description: The death-word interaction is statistically significant omnibus, but none of the attempt-versus-other pairwise contrasts are significant. The manuscript appropriately notes this, but inclusion among significant temporal findings risks overstating relevance to attempts; the omnibus may reflect differences among non-attempt conditions.
issues.quote: There was also a significant interaction for death words, 2(3)=9.47, p=.024. However, there were no significant differences in change over time for attempt compared to all other episodes

issues.subcategory: clinical-monitoring implications exceed evidence
issues.description: The clinical implications discuss a tool monitoring communication behind the scenes and notifying clinicians/family, but the study did not estimate sensitivity, specificity, false positives, false negatives, calibration, acceptability, or intervention outcomes. These claims are speculative and should be more clearly separated from empirical findings.
issues.quote: Knowledge gained from this study could put us one step closer to the development of an objective monitoring tool capable of tracking individuals’ communication “behind the scenes,” notifying suicidal individuals and/or their clinician or family if their patterns of communication indicate increasing levels of suicide risk.
